article.title: Why “No Significant Difference” Does Not Mean “The Same”
article.why: Practical analytical English for data-driven decisions.

paragraphs.en: An experiment produces a p-value above 0.05, and the report says, “There is no difference between A and B.” That conclusion is often too strong. A non-significant result means the data did not provide sufficient evidence to reject the null hypothesis under the chosen test and assumptions. It does not prove that the two options are identical. Sample size is one reason. If an outcome is rare or the experiment is small, the test may have low power to detect a difference that matters to the business. The confidence interval may include zero but also include meaningful positive and negative effects. In that situation, the result is uncertain rather than evidence of sameness. Confidence intervals help because they show the range of effect sizes compatible with the data under the model assumptions. Suppose the estimated lift is one percentage point with an interval from minus two to plus four. The test may be non-significant, but the data still allow effects that could matter. If the business question is whether two options are practically equivalent, an equivalence test is more appropriate. The team first defines an equivalence margin: the largest difference considered too small to matter. The analysis then asks whether the confidence interval is sufficiently contained within that margin. This reverses the usual logic. Instead of asking whether there is evidence of any difference, it asks whether sufficiently large differences can be ruled out. Non-inferiority designs use related logic when the goal is to show that a new option is not unacceptably worse than a reference. These margins should be defined before seeing the results and should reflect business or clinical relevance rather than convenience. Reporting language matters. “We found no statistically significant difference” accurately describes the test. “The two versions perform the same” requires stronger evidence. Good decisions depend on effect size, uncertainty, sample size, and the range of differences that would actually change the decision. Analysts should state the population, denominator, observation window, and decision rule before interpreting the result. A useful review separates the observed metric from the mechanism that produced it and from the action that should follow. This makes the conclusion easier to reproduce, challenge, and communicate. paragraphs.zh: 繁中完整翻譯與解說：本文強調，指標本身不足以支撐決策。解讀百分比、彙總結果、model drift、非顯著結果或分類 threshold 時，都必須同時確認母體、分母、比較基準、統計不確定性以及實際 business cost。只有把觀察結果與資料生成機制、決策條件分開，才能避免過度解讀。
paragraphs.ja: 日本語完全訳・解説：percentage、集計値、model drift、非有意な結果、classification thresholdは、数値だけでは意思決定を支えられない。母集団、分母、比較基準、統計的不確実性、business costを確認し、観察結果とdata generating mechanism、decision ruleを分けて解釈する必要がある。
